A beam from a **distant source**, or a collimated laser beam, has a **plane** wavefront.
**Step 1 — recall what a wavefront is.** It is the surface joining all points of the wave
that are in the **same phase** ✓ and it is always **perpendicular** to the direction in
which the light travels.
**Step 2 — think about a parallel beam.** All its rays travel in the **same direction**,
so the surface perpendicular to every one of them is a **flat plane** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** The initial wavefront is **planar** ✓
**How wavefronts relate to their sources.**
a **point source** gives **spherical** wavefronts, expanding outwards
a **line source** gives **cylindrical** wavefronts
a source at **infinity**, or a collimated beam, gives **plane** wavefronts ✓
A sphere of very large radius is locally indistinguishable from a plane, which is exactly
why light from a distant star arrives at the Earth as a plane wave.
**Why this matters.** Almost all of interference and diffraction theory assumes plane
waves arriving at the slits ✓ Young's double slit, the diffraction grating and Huygens'
constructions all start from a plane wavefront, which is why experiments use a distant
source or a collimating lens.
**What a lens does to it.** A converging lens turns an incoming **plane** wavefront into
a **converging spherical** one centred on the focus ✓ That is the wave-optics way of
saying that a lens brings parallel rays to a point.
**Why a laser beam qualifies.** Its light is emitted into a very narrow cone, so across
the beam the rays are parallel to a high degree ✓ Over long distances the beam does
spread slightly by diffraction, and the wavefront becomes gently curved - but initially
it is flat.
**Reading the distractors.** **Concave** ✗ would describe a **converging** beam heading
for a focus; **convex** ✗ a **diverging** beam from a nearby point source. Neither is a
parallel beam. **Convex near the axis and concave near the periphery** ✗ describes no
physical wavefront at all ✓
∴ planar.

In a metamaterial the refractive index is **negative**, but the speed of light is set by
its **magnitude**.
**Step 1 — recall the definition.** The refractive index relates the speed in vacuum to
the speed in the medium:
**v = c/|n|** ✓
**Step 2 — see why the modulus is needed.** A speed is a **positive** quantity ✓ If n is
negative, writing v = c/n would give a negative speed, which is meaningless. The sign of
n describes the **direction** in which the wavefronts move relative to the energy, not
the rate at which light travels.
**Step 3 — conclude.** **v = c/|n|** ✓
**What a negative index means physically.** A metamaterial has both **permittivity** and
**permeability** negative over some band of frequencies ✓ Light entering it is refracted
to the **same** side of the normal as the incident ray - the opposite of ordinary
refraction - and the phase velocity runs **backwards** relative to the energy flow. These
are engineered structures, not natural materials.
**What happens to the wavelength.**
λ_medium = λ_air/|n| ✓
so the wavelength is **shortened**, exactly as in an ordinary medium of index |n|. This
is why the option claiming λ_m = λ_air|n| is wrong: it would **lengthen** the wavelength
in a dense medium.
**Why such materials are interesting.** A slab of index −1 can act as a **flat lens**
with no curvature, and can in principle beat the ordinary diffraction limit ✓ They are
also the basis of cloaking devices, which bend light around an object.
**A worked instance.** For n = −1·5:
v = 3 x 10⁸/1·5 = **2 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹** ✓ the same speed as in ordinary glass of index +1·5
λ in the material = λ_air/1·5 ✓ also the same as in glass
What differs is the **direction** of refraction, not these magnitudes.
**Reading the distractors.** **v = c|n|** ✗ would exceed c for any |n| > 1, violating
relativity. **v = c** ✗ ignores the medium entirely. **λ_m = λ_air|n|** ✗ reverses the
wavelength relation ✓
∴ the speed of light in the meta-material is v = c/|n|.

In a series LCR circuit the voltages across the three components do **not** add
arithmetically - L and C are in antiphase, so they subtract first.
**Step 1 — note the phase relationships.**
V_R is **in phase** with the current
V_L **leads** the current by 90°
V_C **lags** the current by 90°
so V_L and V_C are **180° apart** and partly cancel ✓
**Step 2 — combine the reactive voltages.**
V_L − V_C = 60 − 30
= **30 V**
**Step 3 — add this to V_R in quadrature.** The resultant reactive voltage is
perpendicular to V_R in the phasor diagram:
V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²)
= √(40² + 30²)
= √(1600 + 900)
= √2500
= **50 V** ✓
**Why the supply voltage is less than the sum.** Adding the three arithmetically gives
60 + 30 + 40 = **130 V** ✗ - the distractor offered. That would be right only if all
three were in phase, which they are not: the inductor and capacitor voltages largely
cancel each other ✓
**The striking feature of LCR circuits.** The voltage across a single component can
**exceed** the supply voltage ✓ Here V_L = 60 V across the inductor while the supply is
only 50 V - an everyday fact in resonant circuits, and the reason such circuits need care.
**A check with a 3-4-5 triangle.** V_R = 40 and the net reactive voltage 30 form the two
short sides of a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 10, so the hypotenuse is **50** ✓
**The phase angle, for completeness.**
tan φ = (V_L − V_C)/V_R = 30/40 = 0·75
**φ = 36·9°**, with the current **lagging** the voltage, since V_L > V_C and the circuit
is net inductive ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **130 V** ✗ adds all three as scalars. **70 V** ✗ is
60 + 40 − 30 or similar partial cancellation. **10 V** ✗ is 40 − 30, forgetting the
quadrature addition ✓
∴ 50 V.

Combine the inductor and capacitor voltages first - they are in **antiphase** - and then
add the resistor voltage in quadrature.
**Step 1 — read the three voltages from the circuit.**
V_R = **80 V**
V_L = **40 V**
V_C = **100 V**
**Step 2 — find the net reactive voltage.**
V_L − V_C = 40 − 100
= **−60 V**
The magnitude is 60 V, and the negative sign says the circuit is net **capacitive** ✓
**Step 3 — add in quadrature with V_R.**
E = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²)
= √(80² + 60²)
= √(6400 + 3600)
= √10000
= **100 V** ✓
**Why the answer is a round number.** 80 and 60 are the legs of a 3-4-5 triangle scaled
by 20, so the hypotenuse is **100** ✓ Examiners choose such triples deliberately.
**Why it is not 220 V.** Adding all three arithmetically gives 80 + 40 + 100 = 220 V ✗ -
the first distractor, and the error the question is designed to catch. The capacitor and
inductor voltages are 180° apart and cancel to 60 V before anything else is done ✓
**What the circuit is doing.** With V_C > V_L the circuit is **capacitive**, so the
current **leads** the applied emf:
tan φ = (V_L − V_C)/V_R = −60/80 = −0·75
**φ = −36·9°** ✓ the current leads by about 37°.
**Note that V_C alone exceeds the supply.** 100 V appears across the capacitor while the
source supplies 100 V - and with slightly different values V_C could exceed it ✓ This is
normal in a series LCR circuit and is not a violation of anything; the voltages are
phasors, not scalars.
**Reading the distractors.** **220 V** ✗ is the arithmetic sum. **140 V** ✗ is
√(80² + (40+100)²) with the reactive voltages wrongly **added**. **20 V** ✗ is
100 − 80 ✓ Only the quadrature combination gives 100 V.
∴ 100 V.
